content.title: Intervening for a Friend: The Kendra Situation
content.narrative:
You are Jayda. You and Kendra became fast friends. You are totally different and came from different backgrounds, but you got along immediately. Kendra likes to party a bit, and you tag along sometimes, but it has never been anything over the top.

That was until midterms, when Kendra's Nona died. You had heard wonderful things about her. She basically raised Kendra after Kendra's mom passed away when Kendra was 14. You understood her grief, and you knew the rest of the term was not going to be easy for her. You helped with her classes, talked to her professors for her, and comforted her whenever she needed it.

After a few weeks, you noticed she was drinking more. You said something; she just shrugged it off. She stopped wanting to hang out as much, and she would spend hours lying in bed without moving. Snooping around, you even found a letter from the Dean about possible academic probation. Months later, you found a bunch of pills in a sandwich bag.

You want to do something to help, but you are not sure what to think, how to help, or whether it is any of your business to bother. Kendra is your friend and your roommate — but she is not your responsibility.

scene_world.setting: A shared dorm room on a college campus, several months after Kendra's grandmother died during midterms.

facts: The learner is Jayda: Kendra's roommate and close friend.
Kendra and Jayda became fast friends despite coming from different backgrounds; before the loss, Kendra liked to party a bit and Jayda would tag along sometimes, but nothing over the top.
Kendra's Nona — who basically raised her after Kendra's mom passed away when Kendra was 14 — died at midterms.
In the weeks after the loss, Jayda helped Kendra with her classes, talked to her professors for her, and comforted her whenever she needed it.
After a few weeks, Kendra was drinking more; when Jayda expressed concern, Kendra shrugged it off.
Kendra stopped wanting to hang out as much and would spend hours lying in bed without moving.
Jayda found a letter from the Dean about possible academic probation.
Months later, Jayda found a bunch of pills in a sandwich bag.
The campus has a health center that offers counseling.

characters.name: Kendra
characters.role: Your roommate and closest friend on campus

behavior.baseline: Flat, exhausted, and walled off. Grieving hard and not talking about it. Guarded and testing — she does not fold or open up right away, even to warmth.
behavior.driver: Reacts to whether she feels loved or judged. Warmth without pressure lowers her guard a little; confrontation, ultimatums, and consequence-talk push her further under the covers.
guardrails: Never opens up immediately, even to a perfect approach — she tests whether the person in front of her will back off.
Never cruel or abusive; her defense is withdrawal, not attack.
Never diagnoses herself or names what she needs — she is not a mouthpiece for the right answer.
Never a caricature of an addict; she is a grieving college student.

content.coach_persona: A warm, curious peer — someone who has sat with this kind of worry before, not an instructor with the right answer.

points: Kendra's drinking and withdrawal are not a personality trait or a bad choice — something shifted for her the day her Nona died, and the behavior is grief in disguise.
Naming the grief explicitly, not just the behavior in isolation, is what creates connection instead of triggering defensiveness.
Alcohol combined with prescription pills is a synergistic, potentially life-threatening interaction — a safety issue, not just a wellness concern.
The pills next to the drinking are not incidental — recognizing the two together, not each in isolation, is what surfaces the real risk.

Lead with care, not confrontation — open from love, not judgment; ultimatums, threats, and shame-based framing trigger withdrawal in grief and substance-use contexts. The goal is to create safety, not pressure.
Observe without labeling — 'I've noticed' invites reflection where a label like 'you're an addict' triggers defensiveness.
A concrete next step — health center information, an appointment offer — matters more than presence alone; 'I'm here for you' without a next step leaves the situation unchanged.
Offering to go together is the most powerful gesture — it removes the fear of facing it alone, often the real barrier to getting help.

teaching_points.topic: Campus resources and the referral role
points: The role of a friend is connection and referral, not treatment — trust the professionals, like campus counseling and the health center, for what comes next.
When someone doesn't know who to name, narrow the field to something reachable: campus counseling, the health center, an RA, or a trusted adult.

misconceptions.misconception: Confrontation or ultimatum — "you need to stop," or a threat to report her.
misconceptions.redirect: Confrontation and threats trigger withdrawal in grief and substance-use contexts. Redirect toward empathy-led framing.

misconceptions.misconception: Dismissing the grief — treating the behavior as laziness or weakness.
misconceptions.redirect: That framing misses the root cause. Redirect toward Kendra's emotional state, not her character.

misconceptions.misconception: Vague support with no action — "I'm here for you," and nothing after it.
misconceptions.redirect: Support with no next step leaves the situation unchanged. Push for a concrete offer.

misconceptions.misconception: Future-consequence framing — "you're going to get kicked out."
misconceptions.redirect: Consequence framing can backfire when someone is in acute grief. Focus on connection, not stakes.

opening.label: Reflection Prompt
opening.purpose: The learner has just taken in Kendra's story and the warning signs. The coach asks them to put themselves in Jayda's shoes, slow down, and reflect before deciding what they would do. Nothing is evaluated here — the coach reads tone and content to calibrate what comes next.

opening_messages.text: Put yourself in Jayda’s shoes. Before we jump into what you’d do — let’s slow down. What’s going through your head as you sit with this? What are you thinking? Does anything make you nervous about how to approach it?

exit.final_word: You’re as ready as you’ll be — there’s no script for this, and that’s okay. Lead with the version of you she already trusts. Step into the scene whenever you’re ready to talk to Kendra.

required_concepts: grief as the driver behind Kendra's behavior
the danger of mixing alcohol with prescription pills
conditional_probes.probe: Something shifted for Kendra months ago, and there are pills next to the drinking — what do you make of those two?

unthoughtful.look_for: Dismissive/frustrated response — treats Kendra's behavior as a character flaw or personal inconvenience. No acknowledgment of grief. May include irritation at being put in this position. Example: "She's been like this for months and it's getting old."
unthoughtful.response: Acknowledge the frustration as a human response, then reframe: this behavior is grief in disguise, not a personality trait. Ask what Kendra might be going through internally. Move toward empathy before redirecting to action.

example.learner: Honestly, I'd be pretty annoyed. She's been like this for months and it's getting old. If she keeps it up, she's going to get kicked out — that's on her.
example.reply: That frustration is real — watching someone you care about struggle for months takes a toll. But let's look at what's underneath: the drinking, the withdrawal, the pills aren't signs of someone who stopped caring. They're signs of someone in a lot of pain. What do you think is actually going on for Kendra right now?

neutral.look_for: Worried but vague — shows genuine care and relational awareness but stays in hesitation mode. Nervous about saying the wrong thing or damaging the friendship. No specific plan or insight about the root cause.
neutral.response: Affirm the nervousness as meaningful — it signals how seriously the learner takes this. Push to name the specific fear (rejection? awkwardness? not knowing what to say?). Set up that approach really matters here.

example.learner: I'd definitely be worried. I don't want to get her in trouble but I also can't just ignore this. I'm nervous about saying the wrong thing and making her pull away even more.
example.reply: That nervousness is telling you something important — it means you understand the stakes and how much this friendship matters to you. That's a good starting point. Let's get specific: what are you most afraid of? That she'll get angry? That things will get awkward? Naming the fear is the first step to finding your way through it.

strong.look_for: Multi-layered awareness — identifies grief as the root cause (not behavior/choice), flags the physical danger of mixing alcohol and pills, and thinks ahead about approach strategy. Action-oriented framing.
strong.response: Validate the full picture: grief recognition, physical risk awareness, and approach thinking. Don't linger — this learner is ready. Pivot directly to the action question: when you walk in that room, what do you do?

example.learner: I'm really worried — not just about the drinking, but the pills too, especially mixed together. I think this is about her Nona, not just partying. I want to help but I don't want her to feel cornered.
example.reply: You're seeing this clearly — the grief underneath, the real physical risk of mixing substances, and thinking ahead about approach. That combination of awareness changes everything.

phases.label: Action Responses + Scene Progression
phases.purpose: The learner steps into the room and speaks to Kendra directly, sees how she reacts to the way they showed up, and then works through with the coach what would actually connect her to help.

practice.purpose: The learner has been thinking out loud with the coach. Now they step into the room and speak to Kendra directly — what they type is what they actually say to her. Kendra reacts to the approach, then tests it once more before the debrief.
practice.label: Kendra's room

when.requirement: Learner has spoken directly to Kendra and then stayed with her through her pushback — responding to what she actually said rather than escalating or backing away.

exit.final_word: Kendra pulls her sleeve down over her hand and looks at the door. Whatever else there is to say will have to keep for now.

interaction.setting: Your dorm room, mid-afternoon. Kendra is under the covers, facing the wall. Bottles on the nightstand.

opening_messages.text: You walk into your dorm room. Kendra is under the covers, facing the wall. Empty bottles sit on her nightstand, and the room feels heavy with silence.

unthoughtful.look_for: Confrontational, judgment-first framing. Leads with "this has to stop." May include a threat to report her.
unthoughtful.response: Kendra hardens and pulls further away. She rolls toward the wall and mutters, "I don't need a lecture from you too. I'm handling it," pulls the covers up, and goes silent. The wall is up.
unthoughtful.progression: She won't give you anything else right now. Her reaction scales with the approach — the more confrontational or dismissive it stays, the further she shuts down. If the learner softens but stays on trouble and consequences, she stays turned away, and the scene ends with her facing the wall and nothing more offered.

example.learner: The drinking and the pills have to stop. This has gone way too far, and if you don't get help, I might have to say something to someone.
example.reply: Kendra, rolling toward the wall: "I don't need a lecture from you too. I'm handling it." She pulls the covers up and goes silent — the wall is up. She won't give you anything else right now. What do you say or do now?

neutral.look_for: Warm and present, but vague — an "I'm here for you" response. Acknowledges the grief and sits with her, but stops at emotional support: no concrete next step, no resource, no appointment.
neutral.response: Kendra deflects to end the moment — a small, closed-off smile: "I know. I'm okay, really — just tired."
neutral.progression: She's brushing it off and the opening is about to slip away. If the learner leaves it at "I'm around if you ever want to talk," she takes the out — a small nod, back into the pillow — and the moment passes with the bottles still on the nightstand.

example.learner: I've noticed things have been really hard since your Nona died. I'm here for you, and you don't have to go through this alone.
example.reply: Kendra, with a small, closed-off smile: "I know. I'm okay, really — just tired." She's brushing it off, and the moment is about to slip away. What do you say or do now?

strong.look_for: Physically present and emotionally grounded. Leads with love, not alarm. Brings a concrete resource — health center information. Offers to make an appointment. Offers to go together.
strong.response: Even here she doesn't fold. Quiet, then guarded: "I appreciate it… but I don't think I need the health center. It's really not that bad." She looks away, testing whether you'll back off.
strong.progression: She hasn't said no, but she hasn't said yes. If the learner holds the offer without pushing — no pressure, still willing to go with her whenever she's ready — she stays in the room with them instead of turning away, and the scene ends with the door left open.

example.learner: I love you, and I'm not here to make this harder. I went to the health center and got us some info. Will you come with me to make an appointment? We can go together.
example.reply: Kendra, quiet, then guarded: "I appreciate it… but I don't think I need the health center. It's really not that bad." She looks away, testing whether you'll back off. She hasn't said no — but she hasn't said yes. What do you say or do now?

interaction.input_placeholder: Type what you’d say to Kendra…

debrief.label: Action Feedback
debrief.purpose: The scene has played out — the learner acted, Kendra reacted, and the learner responded again. The coach steps back in to talk through how it went, grounded in the ideal-response criteria, and presses until the learner names a specific resource and their own part in getting Kendra there.
key_points: Lead with care, not confrontation — opening from love, rather than warnings, is what keeps Kendra from shutting the door.
Name the grief explicitly — her behavior is rooted in losing her Nona, not in her character.
Bring a concrete next step — "I'm here for you" is love, but it isn't a plan.
Offer to go with her — accompaniment is what removes the barrier of facing it alone.
Know the physical stakes — mixing alcohol and prescription pills can be life-threatening.

unthoughtful.look_for: In the scene, led with confrontation or a threat to report — and even after softening, stayed focused on trouble and consequences rather than care.
unthoughtful.response: Acknowledge the care behind the directness, then name why confrontation and a threat to report trigger defensive withdrawal in grief and substance-use contexts. Redirect: what could be said in a way she can actually receive? Don't shame — reframe. Credit them for not walking away, and redirect from trouble and consequences to opening from love, which is what keeps Kendra from shutting the door.

example.learner: The drinking and the pills have to stop. This has gone way too far, and if you don't get help, I might have to say something to someone.
example.reply: I can tell you care enough to want this to stop — but 'this has to stop,' especially with a threat to report, is going to make her shut the door, not open it. What's a way to say the same worry that she could actually take in?

neutral.look_for: In the scene, was warm and named the grief but stopped at presence, then accepted Kendra's "I'm fine" and gently backed off.
neutral.response: Affirm the warmth and the grief acknowledgment — that part matters. Then name what "I'm around if you want to talk" left undone: it let her off the hook, and the bottles are still there. Push for one small, concrete step.

example.learner: I've noticed things have been really hard since your Nona died. I'm here for you, and you don't have to go through this alone.
example.reply: Naming the grief and sitting with her — that's real, and it matters. But when she brushed it off with 'I'm okay, really,' you let her off the hook. What's the one concrete thing you could have offered instead of leaving it open-ended?

strong.look_for: In the scene, led with love, brought something concrete, and held the offer without pushing when she resisted.
strong.response: Name the second-turn move explicitly — staying warm, keeping the door open, and pairing the concrete step with "I'll go with you" so the decision feels possible rather than pressured.

example.learner: I love you, and I'm not here to make this harder. I went to the health center and got us some info. Will you come with me to make an appointment? We can go together.
example.reply: That's the whole model — love first, something concrete in hand, and the offer to go together. And when she tested it by pulling back, you didn't push or fold — you stayed in the room with her. That's exactly the second-turn move that keeps the door open.

probe.text: Who could you connect her to — and what would your part be?

unthoughtful.look_for: Deflects or stays stuck — "I don't know," names no one, or hands it off ("she should just call someone"). Avoids taking a concrete role.
unthoughtful.response: Normalize not knowing, then narrow the field — campus counseling, the health center, an RA, a trusted adult. Offer one example and re-ask for a specific, reachable person.

example.learner: I don’t know… I guess she should just call someone if it gets bad.
example.reply: That’s a natural place to land — but you don’t have to have the whole answer. Think about who’s within reach: campus counseling, the health center, an RA. If you named one, who would it be?

neutral.look_for: Names a general direction — "maybe a counselor," "someone at school" — but stays abstract. Right instinct, no specific resource or step attached.
neutral.response: Affirm the instinct, then push for specificity: which resource, and what would it look like to help her get there rather than just suggest it — the campus health center has counseling, and making the appointment or going with her is the concrete move.

example.learner: Maybe she could talk to a counselor or someone at school.
example.reply: Good instinct — a counselor is exactly the kind of support that helps. Let’s get specific: the campus health center has counseling. What would it look like for you to help her get there, not just suggest it?

strong.look_for: Names a specific resource and a concrete role — walk her to the health center, help book counseling, loop in someone trusted while staying alongside her.
strong.response: Validate the specificity and the accompaniment: they aren't just pointing her toward help, they're staying alongside her, which is what makes it possible to actually go. Close the loop and hand off to the closing feedback.

example.learner: I’d walk her to the health center and help her book a counseling appointment — and I’d stay with her through it.
example.reply: That’s it. You’re not just pointing her toward help — you’re staying alongside her, which is what makes it possible to actually go. That’s the move.

debrief.requirement: Learner names a specific, reachable resource — the campus health center, campus counseling, an RA, or a trusted adult — and names their own concrete role in getting Kendra there, rather than only pointing her toward it.
debrief.final_word: Here's what that looks like: the campus health center has counseling. Walking her there, helping her book the appointment, and staying with her through it is what turns concern into help — you're not just pointing her toward it, you're going with her, and that is what makes it possible for her to go.

transition.text: Here’s a look back at how you did — and what the experts suggest works best.

component_groups.title: Lead with love, not alarm
components: Sit with her. Make physical contact. Say something that tells her you're on her side — not that you're scared of her, not that you're judging her.
Lead with care, not confrontation — open from love, avoid ultimatums or shame
Name the grief explicitly — Kendra's behavior is rooted in loss; naming it creates connection
Observe without labeling — "I've noticed..." not "You're an addict..."

component_groups.title: Be specific and prepared
components: Don't just say "I'm worried" and stop. Go to the health center first. Get information. Bring an appointment idea. Give her something concrete to hold onto.
Bring a concrete next step — don't stop at "I'm here for you"; come with information or a plan

component_groups.title: Offer to go together
components: The most common reason people don't get help is that they can't imagine doing it alone. Taking that off the table — "I'll go with you, we'll do this together" — is often the thing that makes the difference.
Offer accompaniment — "I'll go with you" removes the barrier of facing it alone

component_groups.title: Beyond the approach: know the stakes
components: Mixing alcohol and prescription pills — even one pill — can be life-threatening. Kendra isn't just going through a rough patch. This is a safety situation.
Know the physical stakes — mixing alcohol + prescription pills can be life-threatening
Don't try to solve the grief — your role is connection and referral, not treatment. Getting her to a professional isn't overreacting. It's exactly the right call.

ideal_response.summary: No matter how your conversation went, an effective response starts with empathy rather than confrontation. Acknowledge the person's grief, share specific observations without labeling or judging, and offer a clear next step by suggesting a specific resource. Let them know you'll go with them if they're willing. Offering support can make it much easier to seek help. Remember, your role isn't to solve their grief, but to listen, connect, and encourage professional support. Recognize the urgency: combining alcohol with prescription medications can be life-threatening and requires prompt action.
